samples.summary: Operator-facing self-hosting guide never mentions the new GOOGLE_* variables or a Google OAuth setup procedure
samples.evidence: The canonical self-hosting doc lists `GITHUB_CLIENT_ID` / `GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET` / `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` in its required-env table (lines 127-143) and has a dedicated "GitHub OAuth Setup" section (line 431), but a repo-wide grep for `GOOGLE` returns no hit in this file. The change documents the new vars only in `docs/design/backend.md` and `packages/backend/README.md`, so a self-hosting operator following the published guide has no documented way to discover or enable the feature this change exists to ship.
searchedFor: Grep GOOGLE across repo (no hit in packages/documentation)
Grep GITHUB_CLIENT_ID across repo → self-hosting.md, backend/README.md, README.md, docs/design/backend.md

samples.summary: Documented cookie-Secure resolution order is now wrong: it still says only GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL is consulted
samples.evidence: `isSecureCookie()` now loops over `['GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL','GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL']` (packages/backend/src/auth/oauth-state.ts:244), but self-hosting.md's "Cookies, TLS and the callback URL" section still documents step 2 as "`GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` starts with `https://` → secure; `http://` → not secure" and step 3 as "no callback URL configured at all". An install that sets `GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL=http://…` now silently drops `Secure`/`__Host-` in a case the published doc says falls through to NODE_ENV — the exact misconfiguration this section exists to prevent. Same staleness in `docs/design/backend.md:839` (NODE_ENV row: "fallback … when `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` is unset").
searchedFor: Grep GOOGLE in docs/design/backend.md env table

samples.summary: The verified-flag predicate is copy-pasted into both strategies instead of shared, in a change whose stated principle is sharing the cross-provider auth logic
samples.evidence: `isVerifiedFlag` (google.strategy.ts:21-23) and `isFlagSet` (github.strategy.ts, `return value === true || (typeof value === 'string' && value.trim().toLowerCase() === 'true')`) are byte-identical predicates. The same change introduces `web-oauth-login.ts` precisely so "the one check that stops login CSRF has one implementation"; the verified-email check is described in the design doc as equally load-bearing across providers, yet its parsing rule is duplicated and free to diverge (e.g. a future `"1"` acceptance landing in one file only).

samples.summary: GitHub verified-email enforcement is scope beyond "add Google sign-in" and can lock out existing users
samples.evidence: `validate` now throws `UnauthorizedException` when no verified GitHub address exists, and the strategy requests `allRawEmails: true`. This changes behavior for the provider every install already uses: an existing user whose GitHub primary address is unverified (GitHub's default state for some accounts) loses access at next login, with no migration note in the docs beyond the risk paragraph. It is defensible as the other half of the email-merge safety argument, but it is an unrequested behavior change riding along with the Google feature and should at minimum be called out as a breaking change for operators.
searchedFor: Grep GITHUB_USER_EMAIL_URL / self-hosting.md for any migration note

samples.summary: `GET /auth/providers` hardcodes `github: true` rather than deriving it
samples.evidence: `authProviders()` returns `{ github: true, google: googleAuthConfigured() }`. Google gets a configured-check helper in `oauth-providers.ts` while GitHub is asserted unconditionally; a deployment missing `GITHUB_CLIENT_ID` still advertises a button that fails at GitHub. The design doc justifies it ("GitHub is not optional"), so this is a consistency preference rather than a defect.
